title: Bootstrapping a Cluster with kubeadm
intro: Every kubeadm cluster starts the same way: initialize the first control plane node, install a pod network, then join worker nodes to it. This is the setup tutorial-025's upgrades and tutorial-023's disaster recovery both assume already happened once.

steps.prompt: Initialize the first control plane node, telling it what pod CIDR range to use for the network you'll install next.
steps.fake_output:
[init] Using Kubernetes version: v1.30.1
[certs] Generating certificates and keys...
[control-plane] Creating static pod manifests...
[bootstrap-token] Using token: abc123.def456ghi789jkl0
Your Kubernetes control-plane has initialized successfully!

To start using your cluster:
  mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
  cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config

Then you can join any number of worker nodes by running:
  kubeadm join 10.0.0.1:6443 --token abc123.def456ghi789jkl0 --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:aaaa...
steps.explanation: This single command generates all the control-plane certificates, starts the static pods (etcd, apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager) from tutorial-024, and prints the exact join command for workers.
steps.why: --pod-network-cidr has to be specified up front because it can't be changed after the fact without re-initializing — get it wrong here and you're redoing this step, so it needs to match whatever CNI plugin you're about to install.

steps.prompt: Copy the admin kubeconfig so you can actually use kubectl as a normal user instead of root.
steps.explanation: kubeadm init generates this file with full cluster-admin credentials — copying it to the default kubeconfig location is what makes plain 'kubectl' work without extra flags.
steps.why: This is the one step that's just file copying, not a kubectl or kubeadm command at all — it's easy to skip and then wonder why kubectl says 'connection refused' even though the cluster genuinely initialized fine.

steps.prompt: The cluster has no pod network yet, which is why core pods are stuck Pending. Install a CNI plugin (Flannel, matching the pod CIDR from step 1).
steps.fake_output:
namespace/kube-flannel created
serviceaccount/flannel created
configmap/kube-flannel-cfg created
daemonset.apps/kube-flannel-ds created
steps.explanation: Kubernetes doesn't ship a pod network implementation — kubeadm init leaves CoreDNS and other pods Pending until something (Flannel, Calico, Cilium...) is installed to actually let pods talk to each other across nodes.
steps.why: Notice this installs as a DaemonSet — one CNI pod per node, same pattern as the log-agent DaemonSet from earlier, since networking setup genuinely needs to happen on every node individually.

steps.prompt: On a separate worker node, join it to the cluster using the token from step 1's output.
steps.fake_output:
[preflight] Running pre-flight checks
[kubelet-start] Starting the kubelet
This node has joined the cluster!
steps.explanation: The token and CA cert hash together prove to the joining node that it's really talking to the control plane it thinks it is, not an impostor — this is the same bootstrap-token mechanism from step 1's output.
steps.why: Tokens expire after 24 hours by default — if you're joining a node later than that, you'd need 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' to generate a fresh one instead of reusing an old, expired one.

steps.prompt: Back on the control plane, confirm the new node actually joined and is healthy.
steps.fake_output:
NAME       STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
master     Ready    control-plane   10m   v1.30.1
node-1     Ready    <none>          30s   v1.30.1
steps.explanation: STATUS Ready confirms the new node's kubelet is heartbeating and the CNI plugin successfully set up networking for it too.
steps.why: If this showed NotReady instead, the CNI DaemonSet pod on that specific node would be the first thing to check — a node can join successfully and still show NotReady if its own network setup didn't complete.
